title: IaC Tool Landscape: Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Ansible
summary: Comparing the major IaC approaches — including the provisioning-vs-configuration-management split that trips up most people new to the space.

slides.markdown:
The split that confuses most people entering this space.

| | Provisioning | Configuration management |
|---|---|---|
| Answers | "What infrastructure should exist" | "What should be installed/configured on it" |
| Tools | Terraform, CloudFormation | Ansible, Chef, Puppet |
| Unit of work | A VM, a VPC, a load balancer | Packages, files, services on an existing machine |

Terraform can create a VM; it has no native concept of "install nginx and start it." Ansible can install nginx on a VM; it has no native concept of "create a VM." They solve adjacent, not competing, problems.

CloudFormation (AWS), ARM/Bicep (Azure), and Deployment Manager (GCP) are each **single-cloud, first-party** tools — deeply integrated, often day-one support for a new service. Terraform is **multi-cloud** via its provider plugin model — one tool, one language across AWS, GCP, Azure, and hundreds more, at the cost of occasionally lagging a brand-new feature until the plugin catches up.

The trade-off: single-cloud shops sometimes prefer the native tool; anyone spanning providers leans Terraform.

**Pulumi** provisions infrastructure using **general-purpose languages** (Python, TypeScript, Go) instead of a DSL like HCL — real loops, functions, and the language's own package ecosystem, executed against the same category of provider plugins Terraform uses.

The trade-off: full language power (unit tests, IDE autocomplete, abstractions your team knows) versus HCL's constrained-but-predictable simplicity — general-purpose code is also easier to write cleverly and hard to reason about, which HCL's limits mostly prevent.

Ansible operates over SSH (or WinRM) against already-existing machines, running **playbooks** — YAML describing desired configuration (packages, files, services) — idempotently, similar in spirit to Terraform but at the OS/application layer instead of the cloud-resource layer.

In a combined pipeline, Ansible typically runs **after** provisioning: Terraform's output (a VM's IP, say) feeds directly into Ansible's inventory, so configuration runs against exactly the machine that was just created, without hand-copying an IP between the two tools.

slides.subTitle: Terraform provisions, Ansible configures
slides.markdown:
Terraform creates a VM and outputs its IP (`output "web_ip" { value = aws_instance.web.public_ip }`). A pipeline step captures that output into an Ansible inventory file, then runs a playbook against it: install nginx, copy an app's config, start the service. Terraform never touches what's installed on the VM; Ansible never creates or destroys the VM itself.

This split also shows up when re-running: re-`apply`-ing Terraform with no infra changes is a no-op, and re-running the Ansible playbook against an already-configured VM is a no-op too — both layers are idempotent, independently.

The **AWS CDK** shares Pulumi's core idea -- write infrastructure in a general-purpose language (TypeScript, Python, Java) -- but takes a different path under the hood: CDK code **synthesizes CloudFormation templates**, which AWS's own CloudFormation service then applies. Pulumi instead talks to provider APIs directly through its own engine and state model.

The practical difference: CDK is AWS-only (it's a code generator for CloudFormation) but inherits CloudFormation's day-one support for new AWS features, while Pulumi is multi-cloud but adds its own layer between your code and each provider's API.

slides.sectionTitle: Crossplane: provisioning through the Kubernetes control plane
slides.markdown:
**Crossplane** takes a different architectural bet entirely: instead of a CLI tool that runs `plan`/`apply`, it extends Kubernetes with **custom resources** representing cloud infrastructure (a `Database` CRD that provisions an actual RDS instance) and a controller that reconciles them continuously, the same reconcile-loop model Kubernetes already uses for Pods and Deployments.

This makes infrastructure provisioning a natural fit for GitOps tooling (Argo CD, Flux) that already knows how to sync Kubernetes manifests -- a team already running GitOps for app deploys can manage cloud infrastructure through the exact same pull-based, continuously-reconciled model, rather than bolting a separate Terraform pipeline on the side.

slides.sectionTitle: The real cost of choosing wrong: switching is a rewrite
slides.markdown:
Unlike most tooling decisions, picking an IaC tool is close to a one-way door once real infrastructure exists. State files, module structure, and CI wiring are all tool-specific -- migrating a few thousand resources from Terraform state to Pulumi (or the reverse) isn't a config tweak, it's importing every resource individually into a new state model and re-verifying nothing changes underneath.

The practical implication: weigh long-term team fit (which language your engineers already write, which cloud(s) you actually run on) heavily over a tool's newest feature, since the cost of a wrong choice compounds with every resource added afterward, not just at initial setup.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: three IaC tools across three teams
slides.markdown:
A common organic failure mode at growing companies: team A adopted Terraform early, team B started with CDK because they were AWS-only and TypeScript-heavy, and team C bolted on Pulumi for a new project. Nobody chose this on purpose -- each decision was locally reasonable -- but the org now needs expertise in three tools' state models, three sets of CI wiring, and has no single place to answer "what infrastructure exists."

The fix isn't necessarily forcing one tool everywhere (a genuine CDK-vs-Terraform trade-off can justify a split), but making the choice **deliberate and reviewed** at the platform level rather than something each team backs into independently -- and being honest that every additional tool is a permanent multiplier on onboarding and incident-response cost.
